newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: FOCUS - Grain cuts shelved in new EU farm proposal.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Grain cuts shelved in new EU farm proposal.

text.p: Dutch Agriculture Minister Jozias Van Aartsen on Wednesday presented a new compromise EU farm price package for next year, postponing a controversial proposal to slash aid to wheat farmers.

The six-page text, presented on the third day of the annual EU farm price marathon, also contained "sweeteners" on sugar and other farm products and a suspension of cereals set-aside penalties for another two years.
Set-aside is a scheme intended to remove costly grain mountains, under which farmers must take a certain percentage of their land out of production to obtain EU subsidies.
Under so-called penalty set-aside, farmers have to take extra land out of production if they exceed planting limits.

EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler has been insisting on a 1.4 billion Ecus ($1.6 billion) cut in cereals susidies, which mainly benefit wealthy grain producers in Britain, France and Germany, so to help finance extra aid for beef producers hit by the mad cow disease crisis.
The Commission estimated that grain farmers, who already receive the lion's share of EU farm subsidies, were over-paid by 8.5 billion Ecus during the past four years.

But an overwhelming majority of farm ministers disputed this estimate, adding it was unfair to make cereals farmers foot the bill and that there was enough spare cash in the 1997 budget to aid beef producers.
The Dutch compromise described the reduction as "premature" and said it should be discussed as part of future farm reforms.
Changes are needed to cater for the EU expansion eastwards and the next round of World Trade Organisation negotiations.

The Dutch text did, however, make a concession to Fischler's argument that cereals farmers have been over-compensated for cuts in support prices agreed under 1992 reforms. It noted that "market prices have, on balance, been higher than those foreseen at the time of the reform."
Prices soared after bad weather hit crops across the world and grain stocks slumped to the lowest level for 20 years.
Farm ministers and Fischler were on Wednesday discusssing the compromise, which includes concessions to member states on rice, sugar, milk, sheepmeat, processed tomatoes and wine.
